intro.caption: Lesson 2-2 — histograms. Half the audience vanished right in the middle of Clip Squad's newest video. Mei pulls 18 viewer watch times to solve the mystery.

balloons.t: Our new video had 18 test viewers, and almost everyone clicked away mid-video! Why?
I pulled the 18 watch times in seconds. Time to group them into a histogram!
Two viewers stopped at 120 seconds — that's 2:00! Put 120 in the 60–119 bin?
No way! 120 is bigger than 119. It belongs in the 120–179 interval!

pages.caption: In a histogram, intervals must be equal and never overlap. Always check which bin holds a boundary value like 120.

balloons.t: All 18 watch times are listed below. Count how many land in each interval!
The tallest bar goes up to 8! Does that mean viewers left at 8 seconds?
No! The height is the frequency — how many viewers are in that interval.
60-second bins are too wide. Let's cut them in half to 30-second bins!
Now we can see whether the drop happened at the start or end of 120–179.

pages.ch: Boss Gate · Find the Dead Spot

balloons.t: Seven viewers bailed between 120 and 149 seconds! What happened at 2:00?
Okay, fine! I put a two-minute unskippable ad for my own stunt replay right at 2:00!
Dex's self-ad is cut, and viewers are staying to the end. Case closed!

win.caption: A histogram groups numerical data into equal intervals with touching bars. Bar height shows frequency (how many values fall in that bin), and narrower bins reveal sharper patterns.

gates.title: Gate 1 · Bin the Watch Times
hints: Conceptual: every interval must have the same width and no gaps, and every number lands in exactly one interval.
Procedural: check the endpoints carefully. 0–59 stops at 59; 60–119 stops at 119; 120 starts the next bin.

worked.q: In the practice set, how many values are in 60–119?

items.label: Frequency of 120–179:
items.aria: frequency of the 120 to 179 second interval

fb.msg: You left out the two 120s! 120 belongs in 120–179, not 60–119.

items.fbDefault: Count every value from 120 through 179, including both 120s.

items.q: Where does a watch time of 120 seconds go?

options.t: In 60–119, because it is right at 2:00
options.fb: 120 is greater than 119, so it cannot fit in 60–119.

options.t: In 120–179, because 120 is the start of that interval
In both 60–119 and 120–179
options.fb: Every data value can only be counted in one interval.

options.t: Leave 120 out because it is on the border
options.fb: Every value must be counted in the histogram.

gates.pass: Counts locked in: 0–59 (3), 60–119 (5), 120–179 (8), 180–239 (2). All 18 viewers accounted for!

gates.title: Gate 2 · Read the Tallest Bar
hints: Conceptual: the horizontal axis shows the time intervals; the vertical axis (bar height) shows the frequency (how many viewers).
Procedural: never read a bar's height as seconds. Combine bars by adding their frequencies.

steps: Suppose a histogram of clip lengths shows 0–9 s: 4 clips, 10–19 s: 7 clips, 20–29 s: 2 clips.
The tallest bar (height 7) means 7 clips are between 10 and 19 seconds — NOT 7 seconds.
How many clips are at least 10 seconds? Add 7 + 2 = 9 clips.
worked.q: In that practice histogram, how many clips are under 20 seconds?

items.q: Dex looks at the tallest bar (120–179, height 8) and says: 'Viewers left at 8 seconds!' What does the 8 really mean?

options.t: 8 viewers left during the 120–179 second interval
8 is the average watch time in seconds
options.fb: Bar height is a count of viewers (frequency), not a time in seconds.

options.t: The video is 8 minutes long
options.fb: The vertical axis shows frequency — how many viewers — not video length.

options.t: 120 viewers watched for 8 seconds
options.fb: 120–179 is the time interval on the horizontal axis; 8 is the viewer count.

items.label: How many viewers watched at least 120 seconds (120–179 or 180–239)?
items.aria: number of viewers who watched at least 120 seconds

fb.msg: 8 is only the 120–179 bin. Include the 180–239 bin too.
2 is only the 180–239 bin. Include 120–179 as well.

items.fbDefault: Add the frequencies of the 120–179 bar and the 180–239 bar.

gates.pass: Ten viewers made it to at least 120 seconds — and 8 of them bailed inside 120–179!

gates.title: Gate 3 · Compare Bin Widths
hints: Conceptual: narrower intervals show more detail about where values cluster without changing the total count.
Procedural: split 120–179 into 120–149 and 150–179, and count which values land in 120–149.

steps: Split into 0–29 and 30–59: 0–29 gets 10, 22 (2 values); 30–59 gets 35, 41, 50, 58 (4 values).
Notice 2 + 4 = 6 — the total never changes, only the detail.
worked.q: In that practice split, what is the frequency of 30–59?

items.label: With 30-second bins, what is the frequency of 120–149?
items.aria: frequency of the 120 to 149 second bin

fb.msg: Do not forget the two 120s — they belong in 120–149.

items.q: Why did the 30-second histogram help Mei solve the mystery better than 60-second bins?

options.t: Narrower bins showed that 7 of the 8 viewers left right between 120 and 149 seconds
Narrower bins changed the total number of viewers
options.fb: The total is still 18 viewers; only the grouping changed.

options.t: Narrower bins have gaps between the bars
options.fb: Histogram bars always touch because the intervals are continuous.

options.t: Narrower bins hide the peak
options.fb: Narrower bins actually pinpointed the peak even more closely.

gates.pass: Seven viewers quit right between 120 and 149 seconds — right at 2:00!

gates.title: Boss Gate · Find the Dead Spot
gates.prompt: Read the final 30-second histogram (frequencies: 0–29: 1, 30–59: 2, 60–89: 2, 90–119: 3, 120–149: 7, 150–179: 1, 180–209: 2) to close the case.
hints: Conceptual: a histogram shows the shape, peak, and spread of grouped data, but hides individual raw numbers.
Procedural: find the tallest bar for the peak, and remember each bar only gives a count inside a range.

steps: The peak is 10–19 with 6 values. Most values cluster before 20.
You cannot read the exact smallest value (could be 0 or 8) from the histogram alone.
worked.q: Can a histogram tell you the exact maximum value?
worked.a: No — only the interval it is in

items.q: Which statement best describes the watch-time distribution?

options.t: It peaks at 120–149 seconds (7 viewers) and drops sharply after 150 seconds
Every interval has the exact same frequency
options.fb: Frequencies range from 1 to 7 — there is a clear peak.

options.t: Most viewers left before 60 seconds
options.fb: Only 3 viewers left before 60 seconds; most stayed past 120.

options.t: The tallest bar means viewers watched for 7 seconds
options.fb: 7 is the frequency (number of viewers), not 7 seconds.

items.q: Can a histogram alone tell you the exact watch time of the single fastest-leaving viewer?

options.t: Yes, it is always the left edge of the first bar
options.fb: The left edge is the start of the interval (0), not necessarily an actual data value.

options.t: No, because a histogram groups values into intervals and hides individual values
Yes, by multiplying the bar height by the bin width
options.fb: That does not give an individual viewer's time.

options.t: No, unless the bars have gaps between them
options.fb: Gaps do not show individual values; a histogram always groups data.

gates.pass: Peak at 120–149 seconds confirmed, and Dex's sneaky 2:00 replay ad is busted!

journal.heading: Lesson 2-2 — what the watch-time mystery taught us
rows: Histograms group numbers into equal, touching intervals with no gaps or overlaps. A boundary value like 120 goes in 120–179, not 60–119.
The height of each bar counts how many data values fall in that interval — never read bar height as a time or score.
Narrower intervals (30 s instead of 60 s) keep the same total count while revealing sharper peaks.
Because values are grouped into bins, you cannot read an exact individual value from a histogram alone.
journal.quote: "A bar height of 8 means 8 viewers, not 8 seconds. Never mix up the axes!" — Mei

teacher.suggested: Use during or after lesson 2-2 (Represent and Describe Data in a Histogram) as one focused read. Whole-class on a projector, pairs on devices, or independent practice. It covers only this lesson: equal intervals, boundary placement, reading frequency vs. value, and comparing bin widths.
standards: Display numerical data in plots on a number line, including dot plots, histograms, and box plots
